subject_entity.notes: Gnostic-adjacent teacher active in Asia Minor, associated with Ephesus c. 90–120. Distinguished between the earthly Jesus (son of Joseph and Mary) and the heavenly Christ (a divine power that descended at baptism and departed before the crucifixion). Opposed the orthodox understanding of a personal incarnation of the Logos.

object_entity.proposition_label: Christ truly became flesh and truly suffered in the body
object_entity.description: The incarnate Christ was a genuine human being who truly was born, truly suffered, truly died, and truly rose again; not a phantom or appearance as the Docetists claimed.

evidence.notes: Christ descended on Jesus at baptism and departed before crucifixion — no true union of divine and human.

passage.excerpt: A certain Cerinthus in Asia taught that the world was not made by the primary God, but by a Power far separated from him and ignorant of the supreme authority. He maintained that Jesus was not born of a virgin, but was the son of Joseph and Mary according to the ordinary course of human generation. After baptism, Christ descended upon him in the form of a dove from the Supreme Ruler; then he proclaimed the unknown Father and performed miracles. But at last Christ departed from Jesus, and then Jesus suffered and rose again.

passage.excerpt: Gaius, in a dialogue against Proclus the Montanist, speaks of Cerinthus, who by revelations pretended were by a great apostle brought forth marvellous tales. Cerinthus taught that after the resurrection there would be an earthly kingdom of Christ. The apostle John, on one occasion going to bathe, and learning that Cerinthus was within, sprang out of the bath and fled, saying he could not endure being under the same roof as one who denied the truth of the Lord's incarnation.
